extracted.intended_audience: registered patent practitioners (attorneys/agents) who file/pay USPTO fees and counsel clients on entity status
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and procedural requirements governing when and how practitioners may claim micro-entity status with the USPTO, the practitioner's duties of inquiry and diligence under 37 C.F.R. § 11.18 and related rules, and remedial/recordkeeping practices to avoid improper fee payments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Micro entity qualification certification requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: In order to qualify as a micro entity, patent applicants must certify that: (1) the applicant qualifies as a small entity as defined in 37 C.F.R. § 1.27; (2) neither the applicant nor the inventor nor a joint inventor has been named as the inventor or a joint inventor on more than four previously filed patent applications; (3) neither the applicant nor the inventor nor a joint inventor, in the calendar year preceding the calendar year in which the applicable fee is being paid, had a gross income . . . exceeding three times the median household income for that preceding calendar year; and (4) neither the applicant nor the inventor nor a joint inventor has assigned, granted, or conveyed, nor is under an obligation by contract or law to assign, grant, or convey, a license or other ownership interest in the application concerned to an entity that . . . had a gross income . . . exceeding three times the median household income for that preceding calendar year.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See generally 37 C.F.R. § 1.29; MPEP § 509.04. Certification must reflect these specific elements; practitioners present certifications on behalf of applicants and are responsible for the underlying inquiry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Previously filed applications — what counts toward the four-application limit
rubrics_metrics.description: For purposes of the gross income basis, the application filing limit includes: (i) previously filed U.S. nonprovisional applications (e.g., utility, design, plant, continuation, and divisional applications), (ii) previously filed U.S. reissue applications, and (iii) previously filed U.S. national stage applications under the Patent Cooperation Treaty (PCT).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: MPEP § 509.04(a) (“B. Application Filing Limit”). All such applications naming the inventor or a joint inventor are counted toward the application filing limit, whether filed before, on, or after March 19, 2013, and regardless of whether they are pending, patented, or abandoned.

rubrics_metrics.name: Previously filed applications — exclusions from the filing limit
rubrics_metrics.description: The application filing limit does not include: (i) foreign applications; (ii) international (PCT) applications for which the basic U.S. national stage filing fee was not paid; and (iii) provisional applications. Also, where an applicant/inventor assigned all ownership rights as the result of previous employment, that prior application may not count for purposes of determining micro entity status.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See 37 C.F.R. § 1.29(b) and MPEP § 509.04(a). Carefully evaluate assignment and employment relationships when counting prior applications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing and form of certification
rubrics_metrics.description: 35 U.S.C. 123 requires a certification as a condition for an applicant to be considered a micro entity. The certification must be in writing and must be filed prior to or at the time a fee is first paid in the micro entity amount in an application or patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A fee may be paid in the micro entity amount only if it is submitted with, or subsequent to, the submission of a certification of entitlement to micro entity status. See 37 C.F.R. § 1.29(f) and MPEP § 509.04.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ongoing entitlement at each fee payment
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if a micro entity certification was filed earlier, the applicant must still be entitled to micro entity status at the time of each payment of a fee in the micro entity amount.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioners must determine entitlement at the time of all micro-entity fee payments; if entitlement lapses, the applicant must notify the Office and pay the small-entity or undiscounted fee as appropriate (MPEP § 509.04(d)-(e)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty to notify USPTO of loss of micro-entity status
rubrics_metrics.description: If any requirement for micro entity status is no longer met, the applicant must notify the Office of loss of micro entity status and pay the required fee in the small entity or undiscounted amount, as appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See MPEP § 509.04(d) and § 509.04(e). Failure to notify can lead to deficiency notices and potential disciplinary consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remedy for good-faith errors in claiming micro entity status
rubrics_metrics.description: If (a) an applicant or patentee establishes micro entity status in good faith, (b) pays fees as a micro entity in good faith, and (c) later discovers the status was established in error or the Office was not notified of loss of entitlement through error, the error will be excused upon compliance with the separate submission and itemization requirements of 37 C.F.R. § 1.29(k)(1) and the deficiency payment requirement of § 1.29(k)(2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow § 1.29(k) procedures and provide required itemization and deficiency payment to cure honest mistakes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practitioner certification obligations under 37 C.F.R. § 11.18
rubrics_metrics.description: When presenting any paper to the USPTO, the registered practitioner certifies that all statements made on his or her own knowledge are true, and that all statements based on information and belief are believed to be true. Further, to the best of the party's knowledge, information and belief, formed after an inquiry reasonable under the circumstances: (i) the paper is not being presented for any improper purpose; (ii) legal contentions are warranted by existing law or a nonfrivolous argument to change law; (iii) allegations and factual contentions have evidentiary support or are likely to have such support after reasonable investigation; and (iv) denials of factual contentions are warranted on the evidence or reasonably based on lack of information or belief.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A practitioner presenting certifications of entity status must have conducted an inquiry reasonable under the circumstances to support factual assertions in the certification. See 37 C.F.R. § 11.18(b)(1)-(2) and related discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consequences of violating § 11.18 (false/fraudulent statements)
rubrics_metrics.description: Violations of § 11.18 may jeopardize the probative value of the filing; any false or fraudulent statements are subject to criminal penalty under 18 U.S.C. § 1001; a registered practitioner who violates this section may be subject to disciplinary action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioners must ensure accuracy and reasonable inquiry to avoid criminal exposure and disciplinary proceedings (37 C.F.R. § 11.18(b)(1), § 11.18(d)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Diligence obligations under 37 C.F.R. § 11.103
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioner must act with reasonable diligence in representing a client. Examples of lapses include not conducting a reasonable inquiry under § 11.18 prior to claiming micro entity status, failing to have reasonable procedures to corroborate information relied upon to sign micro entity certification forms, presenting incorrect certifications at filing, claiming micro entity status when paying issue fees though not entitled, and failing to notify the USPTO of loss of micro entity status.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See the Joint Legal Conclusions citing 37 C.F.R. § 11.103. Maintain procedures and oversight to meet diligence obligations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on conduct prejudicial to the administration of the patent system (37 C.F.R. § 11.804(d))
rubrics_metrics.description: Engaging in conduct prejudicial to the administration of the USPTO patent process includes, inter alia, not conducting reasonable inquiry before claiming micro entity status, failing to have reasonable corroboration procedures, presenting incorrect certifications, claiming micro entity status when no longer entitled at the time of issue fee payment, and failing to notify the USPTO of loss of status and pay the correct fee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Similar factual failures can be characterized as prejudicial conduct under § 11.804(d) and may support discipline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding improper reliance on foreign associates or non-practitioners without corroboration
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners who rely on information from foreign associates or non-practitioner staff must still conduct a reasonable inquiry under the circumstances; language/cultural barriers or reliance on trained foreign associates do not obviate the practitioner's independent duty to verify entity status.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not treat foreign associates' representations as a substitute for corroboration; implement language-appropriate intake and verification processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Best-practice intake and verification procedures (recommended questionnaire items)
rubrics_metrics.description: Implement an intake questionnaire (in an appropriate language) asking inventors/applicants to: voluntarily list all previous US patent applications in which they have been named as inventors; answer questions pertaining to inventorship under MPEP § 2109; provide information/questions on patentability and on-sale bar issues under AIA 35 U.S.C. § 102; receive information and questions to help decide which entity status to claim (MPEP § 2550); be warned about potential damages from falsely claiming small or micro entity status (Unleashing American Innovators Act of 2022); sign the questionnaire with a handwritten signature; and be informed about ongoing duty to disclose material information to patentability under 37 C.F.R. § 1.56.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Final Order describes these specific questionnaire items as effective measures KA adopted to corroborate entity status and reduce errors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Internal auditing, docketing, and personnel controls
rubrics_metrics.description: Perform internal audits of docketed US applications to proactively correct erroneous micro-entity claims; assign personnel to oversee verification checks; increase docketing staff; ensure the docketing system accurately reflects applications so entity status checks are reliable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Respondent's remedial steps (audit, personnel assignment, process changes) are described as appropriate controls to prevent erroneous micro-entity claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verification at time of fee payment and pre-payment inquiry
rubrics_metrics.description: Before accepting client payment of deficient fees or paying any fees (including expedited exam or issue fees), send an inquiry to confirm the client's eligibility for small or micro entity status and check for any changes in entity status at the time of fee payment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practices should ensure entitlement is confirmed at each micro-entity fee payment, per MPEP § 509.04(d) and the Final Order's recommended procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recordkeeping, notification, and cooperation obligations following inquiries or discipline
rubrics_metrics.description: When required by the Office or settlement, a practitioner may be ordered to (a) cooperate fully with USPTO inquiries into improper filings, (b) provide copies of the Final Order to affiliated entities and their officers/managers, and (c) retain records of notices and steps taken to comply with corrective measures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Final Order imposes these obligations as part of sanctions; practitioners should be prepared to maintain and produce records and to notify relevant parties where required.
